title: Radical amazement
hookLine: Abraham Joshua Heschel called for radical amazement at the ordinary (God in Search of Man)

lines: THE FAUCET. THE SWITCH. THE BREAD.
cards: A faucet. Turn the handle and clean water comes out, cold or hot, whenever you like. A light switch.
A slice of bread. The fact that you woke up this morning, your heart having kept going all night without being asked. None of this makes the news, or gets a second look.
Abraham Joshua Heschel, a Jewish teacher and rabbi, thought that missing second look was one of the deepest problems a person can have. And he had a name for the cure.

teach.b: The name is radical amazement, from his book God in Search of Man. First, what he meant.

Not amazement at the unusual, comets, miracles, record-breaking anything, but at the usual: at the plain fact that there is anything at all, instead of nothing. Radical, in the sense of going all the way to the root.
Second, what it's up against. People grow used to the world, Heschel wrote, and taking it for granted is no small mistake.

teach.h: INDIFFERENCE IS A KIND OF BLINDNESS.
teach.b: He called indifference to the sublime wonder of living the root of sin. Strong words from a gentle writer. For him, losing wonder wasn't a mood problem; it was a way of going blind.
Third, where he found the practice.
Heschel stood inside Jewish tradition, which has blessings for ordinary moments: on waking, on eating bread, on seeing lightning, on hearing thunder.
He saw blessing as a way of refusing to take things for granted, out loud, many times a day. A much older line in the Psalms has the same posture.
In the King James words: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works."

teach.h: A SECOND LOOK AT WHAT'S IN YOUR HAND.
teach.b: Fourth, what it asks of anyone, religious or not: not a trip somewhere spectacular, but a second look at what's already in your hand.
Heschel believed wonder was where awareness of God begins. Others who don't share his faith borrow the phrase anyway, because the ordinary is still sitting there, waiting to be noticed.

how: Readers of Heschel often connect radical amazement to Jewish blessings said over ordinary moments, such as waking, eating bread, or seeing lightning; others take the phrase as an invitation to look again at everyday things.

o: Heschel's phrase for wonder that anything ordinary is here at all

games.q: you want more wonder in your life. Heschel is your teacher. where does he send you?
o: back to the ordinary things already around you.
away from the world, to think alone.
games.why: radical amazement is wonder at the usual. the faucet, the bread, the fact that anything exists at all.

practice: Pick up one ordinary thing within reach, a cup, a key, a spoon, and look at it as if it had just been handed to you for the first time: who made it, and what had to happen for it to be here?
Then take Heschel's step and notice that it exists at all. If you pray, you can let this looking become a blessing in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Radical amazement. Abraham Joshua Heschel's phrase for wonder at the ordinary, all the way to the root: that anything is here at all. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: fearfully and wonderfully made. Amazed at the usual, all the way to the root. A week of wonder, complete.
